title: Survey Overview
text:
Summary of Purpose
The Atlantic sea scallop is one of the most valuable fisheries in the United States (U.S.). The National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) is required to assess the status of sea scallop populations and set catch limits for sea scallops in Atlantic U.S. waters, typically implementing annual or biennial specifications through the New England Fishery Management Council (NEFMC). Monitoring the population status of sea scallops is a top priority for the Population & Ecosystems Monitoring & Analysis Division (PEMAD) at the Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC).
The HABitat CAMera system (HABCAM) is a non-invasive, underwater imaging vehicle towed from the stern of research vessels approximately 2 meters above the seafloor, capturing high-resolution, overlapping stereo images. The camera array is additionally equipped with a compass, CTD, sonar and sensors that survey the seafloor, which can be used for estimates of species abundance, habitat characterization, and biodiversity—giving a holistic view of benthic taxa. This vehicle has been used extensively for surveying the sea scallop resource on Georges Bank and the Mid-Atlantic Bight, as well as collecting data on finfish and habitat.

title: Survey Overview
text: High-resolution stereo imagery capturing sea scallops on the seafloor.

title: Why We Survey
text:
Atlantic sea scallops are one of the largest commercial fisheries in the United States. In 2023, the value of the fishery was $359.5 million.
The Magnuson–Stevens Act fosters the long-term biological and economic sustainability of marine fisheries, including the scallop fishery. Under this act, we help: * Prevent overfishing * Rebuild overfished stocks * Increase long-term economic and social benefits derived from fishing * Ensure a safe and sustainable supply of seafood * Protect habitat that fishery species need to spawn, breed, feed, and grow to maturity
Fisheries-independent data from the HabCam Survey is used in the sea scallop stock assessment to infer how the stock size and composition has changed over time. Since sea scallops live on the sea floor, the HabCam’s towed camera system is an ideal method for understanding the abundance and distribution of this species.
The survey began as a collaboration between the Northeast Fisheries Science Center and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution in 2004 through a Cooperative Institute of the North Atlantic Region agreement. The survey was transitioned to the Northeast Fisheries Science Center in 2012 as part of the Ecosystems Surveys enterprise. The survey typically runs between April and June sampling the Mid-Atlantic Bight and Georges Bank over two legs, each spanning 9 to 10 days.
For many years, the HabCam Survey and the Scallop Dredge Survey were integrated over three survey legs aboard the R/V Hugh Sharp homeported in Lewes, Delaware. With the transition of the Scallop Dredge Survey to an industry vessel in 2023, the HabCam Survey is now completed on the NOAA Ship Henry B. Bigelow.



The HabCam vehicle prepared on deck before deployment.


The primary equipment of the HabCam Survey is the HabCam vehicle. The vehicle houses a suite of sensors and electronics mounted on a frame towed behind the ship via a fiber optic cable. HabCam sensors include stereo cameras and strobes for seabed imaging, and sensors for measuring: * Conductivity * Temperature * Pressure * Oxygen concentration * Turbidity * Chlorophyll * Fluorescent dissolved organic matter (fDOM)
HabCam also uses a side-scan sonar to visualize the seabed and a forward-looking sonar for object avoidance. We tow the vehicle between 5 to 7 knots and it flies approximately 2 meters above the seabed. A pilot manually pays cable in and out to ensure clear visibility of the seafloor and achieve the desired height above the seabed. Scientists annotate images and, using the estimated field of view, derive sea scallop standardized abundances and size compositions.

title: Data Use & Scientific Documents
text:
Data Use
The data is used to develop indices of abundance and size composition of Atlantic sea scallop for the stock assessments. Additional fisheries and ecosystem data collected from the images is also processed for use in future stock and ecosystem assessment needs.
A number of other surveys collect data on scallop distribution, abundance, and size supported by the Center’s Scallop Dredge survey and the Research Set Aside Program (including dredge, video drop camera, and an additional HabCam survey). The intent of these multiple surveys is to increase the accuracy and precision of the sea scallop assessment through thorough fisheries-independent surveys.

title: About the Species: The Atlantic Sea Scallop
text:
Overview & Population Status
The primary Atlantic sea scallop fishery operates along the Atlantic coast from the Mid-Atlantic to the US/Canada border using predominantly paired or single scallop dredges and trawl gear[cite: 9]. Most vessels land scallops as shucked meats (the adductor muscle), though some land whole scallops[cite: 9]. Implementing regulations are found at 50 CFR part 648 subpart D[cite: 9].
According to the 2020 stock assessment, Atlantic sea scallop is not overfished and not subject to overfishing[cite: 9].

title: About the Species: The Atlantic Sea Scallop
text:
Appearance & Biology

Appearance: Scallops are bivalves held together by an adductor muscle[cite: 9]. Shells are saucer-shaped with smooth, scalloped edges[cite: 9]. The upper shell is reddish-pink/brown and the lower shell is white or cream (5–10% are albinos)[cite: 9].
Lifespan: Can live up to 20 years, growing rapidly during their first few years up to ~6 inches[cite: 9].
Reproduction: Reproduce by age 2, producing hundreds of millions of eggs per year during late summer/early fall or spring spawning[cite: 9]. Larvae remain in the water column for 4–6 weeks before settling[cite: 9].
Locomotion: Propel themselves through the water by snapping top and bottom shells open and shut to escape predators like sea stars[cite: 9].




Large Atlantic sea scallop specimen.

title: About the Species: The Atlantic Sea Scallop
text:
Habitat, Range & Management
Atlantic sea scallops are found in the Northwest Atlantic Ocean from Newfoundland to Cape Hatteras, NC[cite: 9]. Adult scallops live in dense “beds” on sandy or gravelly ocean floors at depths of 100 to 300 feet on Georges Bank and the Mid-Atlantic[cite: 9].


Map of US and Canadian scallop resource aggregations and commercial fishing activity.


NOAA Fisheries and the New England Fishery Management Council manage the fishery under the Atlantic Sea Scallop Fishery Management Plan via Total Allowable Catch (TAC), crew limits, rotational closures, Vessel Monitoring Systems (VMS), and Individual Fishing Quotas (IFQs)[cite: 9].

title: About the Species: The Atlantic Sea Scallop
text:
Harvest & Gear Impacts
In 2023, commercial landings totaled 27.4 million pounds of meats valued at $360 million[cite: 9]. Fishermen primarily use turtle deflector-style dredges equipped with 4-inch rings to increase efficiency and allow undersized scallops to escape[cite: 9].


Harvested sea scallops being sorted on deck.

title: Component Reference Table
text:
Attachment
Label
Description




Frame
A
Durable, protective and stable platform designed to carry imaging and sampling equipment close to the seafloor.


Tail
B
Supports the rudder, the elevator (vehicle lift) and the side scan sonar.


Blue View
C
An advanced multibeam imaging or scanning sonar system. It functions like an underwater acoustic camera, using high-frequency sound waves rather than light to generate real-time video-like imagery and 3D point clouds in zero-visibility conditions.


CTD
D
It is the primary instrument package used to measure the essential physical properties of seawater such as Conductivity, Temperature, and depth.


EcoTriplet
E
A multi-parameter optical sensor used to measure light scattering and fluorescence in natural waters.


Main Electronics Bottle
F
A heavy-duty, waterproof cylinder that protects an underwater vehicle’s delicate computers, navigation systems, and sensors from the crushing pressure of the ocean.


Expansion Bottle
G
A reservoir that maintains the internal pressure of a fluid-filled system slightly above the surrounding sea pressure. It allows internal oils to expand and contract as temperatures change, while preventing seawater from leaking into sensitive electronics or motors.


SideScan Sonar
H
An acoustic imaging system mounted on an underwater vehicle. It emits fan-shaped sound waves to the left and right, mapping the seafloor to create highly detailed, photo-like 2D images of the seabed, shipwrecks, and debris.


Cable Tubes
I
Hold the cables going to the sensors, reducing cable drag/chaffing.


Cameras
J
Downward facing stereo cameras which capture images of the seafloor, synchronized with the strobes.


4 - Strobes
K
High-intensity, flashing lights used to aid in vehicle recovery, mark worksites, and provide synchronized illumination for high-resolution imaging.


Altimeter
L
An acoustic instrument that measures the exact vertical distance between the vehicle and the seabed. It sends down sound waves and times how long the pulse takes to bounce back from the ocean floor.


Attitude Sensor
M
Measures its 3D orientation in the water, specifically tracking its pitch (nose up or down), roll (side-to-side tilt), and yaw/heading (compass direction).


Pinger
N
A device that emits repeatable acoustic sound pulses. They are used for tracking a vehicle’s position, guiding it to specific subsea targets, or enabling emergency recovery if the vehicle is lost.


Doors
O
To keep the vehicle straight while towing, two doors are attached to HABCAM (act as a rudder).


Lead Weights
P
They allow the craft to achieve neutral buoyancy, fine-tune its center of gravity, and offset buoyant forces.


Weak Link
Q
An engineered mechanical failure point. It is designed to break intentionally when subjected to a predetermined threshold of force (e.g., getting snagged on rocks or debris) to prevent catastrophic damage to the rest of the vehicle or its tether.

title: Frame Schematics & Physical Envelope
text:
HabCam Frame Schematics

1. System Overview
This slide contains the structural schematics and technical drawings for the frame of the Habitat Mapping Camera System (HabCam)[cite: 8]. The HabCam is an advanced, continuously towed underwater imaging vehicle utilized for high-resolution benthic habitat and marine population surveys[cite: 8]. The frame serves as the foundational chassis, providing structural integrity and spatial orientation for a multi-million-dollar suite of oceanographic sensors[cite: 8].


2. Core Design
Because the HabCam operates just meters above the seafloor in challenging marine environments, its frame is engineered to meet strict operational tolerances[cite: 8]. The core design prioritizes three major factors[cite: 8]: * Hydrodynamic Stability: The geometry of the frame is designed to minimize drag and roll, ensuring a smooth, predictable flight path while being towed via the ship’s winch[cite: 8]. * Durability and Impact Resistance: Constructed from marine grade, corrosion resistant alloys, the frame features a robust roll-cage architecture[cite: 8]. This protects sensitive internal housings from catastrophic damage in the event of an accidental seafloor strike or boulder impact[cite: 8]. * Modularity and Accessibility: The frame must allow for rapid on deck maintenance[cite: 8]. The open architecture design ensures that technical teams (such as the HabCam Lead) can easily access fiber optic terminations, adjust wiring if necessary, and calibrate sensors between deployments[cite: 8].


3. Payload Integration
These schematics detail the mounting points, brackets, and load-bearing structures required to securely integrate the vehicle’s primary payload[cite: 8]. When reviewing the drawings, note the specific integration zones for[cite: 8]: * Primary and secondary high-resolution camera housings[cite: 8]. * Illumination strobes and associated power manifolds[cite: 8]. * Forward-looking obstacle avoidance sonar and altimeters[cite: 8]. * The primary tow-point assembly and fiber optic telemetry housing[cite: 8].


4. Navigating The Schematics
The slide begins with complete, fully assembled isometric views, followed by detailed top, side, and front elevations[cite: 8]. Subsequent sections break down individual sub-assemblies (e.g., the tow-arm mechanism, sensor brackets) and conclude with a comprehensive Bill of Materials (BOM) specifying required alloys, fasteners, and torque tolerances[cite: 8].


5. Materials
To maintain structural integrity during tow operations and cushion mechanical impact, the HabCam chassis and mounting components use the following specifications[cite: 8]: * Primary Structural Frame: 304 Stainless Steel tubular/pipe construction, selected for its high tensile strength, impact toughness, and weldability in structural roll-cage configurations[cite: 8]. * Corrosion Mitigation: Exposed 304 stainless steel components are equipped with sacrificial zinc/aluminum anodes or marine-grade anti-corrosion coatings to protect against pitting and galvanic action in prolonged saltwater immersion[cite: 8]. * Fasteners and Brackets: Passivated 316 / 304 Stainless Steel hardware with anti-seize provisions to prevent galling during on-deck servicing, or storage[cite: 8]. * Pressure Housings: Hard-anodized aluminum or specialized pressure-rated housings for sensitive cameras, strobes, and oceanographic sensors[cite: 8].

title: Cable Harness Specifications & Wiring Schematics
text:
1. System Overview
This slide set contains the electrical schematics, pinout diagrams, cable harness routing plans, and interconnect specifications for the Habitat Mapping Camera System (HabCam)[cite: 8].
As a continuously towed underwater imaging vehicle operating near the seabed, the HabCam relies on oceanographic sensors, imaging systems, and acoustic tools[cite: 8]. The cable harnesses described herein provide the link between the centralized vehicle telemetry housing, power distribution manifolds, and individual payload sensors[cite: 8].

Chanos Cable




Schematic Reference: HabCamV4 - Chanos Cable[cite: 8]
Primary Function: Connects the Chanos in-situ biogeochemical analyzer to the HabCamV4 system for ocean chemistry data collection and sensor power[cite: 8].
Key Specifications: * Connector Configuration: 13-pin circular connector on the vehicle hub end (P1) to a 13-pin circular connector on the Chanos sensor end (P2)[cite: 8]. * Power Conductors: Dual +12 VDC power rails using 18 AWG conductors (#18 WHT and #18 RED) paired with dual 18 AWG ground returns (#18 BLK and #18 GRN)[cite: 8]. * Data & Signal Lines: 24 AWG color-coded twisted pairs for differential communications and control lines[cite: 8]. * Cable Shielding: Pin 2 on both ends is dedicated to the cable screen/shield grounding[cite: 8].

Primary Function: Delivers primary system power, strobe synchronization signals, and high-speed Ethernet data between the central telemetry hub and the main camera system[cite: 8].
Key Specifications: * Connector Configuration: 13-pin circular connector on the hub end (P1) to a 13-pin rectangular connector on the camera housing end (P2)[cite: 8]. * Power & Strobe Conductors: Heavy-gauge 18 AWG conductors dedicated to camera power delivery and strobe pulse timing (#18 RED/BLK for power, #18 WHT/GRN for strobe)[cite: 8]. * Ethernet Data Lines: 8 color-coded 24 AWG conductors forming four twisted pairs for high-speed Ethernet telemetry[cite: 8].

title: Vehicle Sensor Preparation & Assembly Protocols
text:
Detailed Subsystem Preparation & Assembly Instructions

BlueView Forward Looking Sonar (1x)



Preparation & Mounting Steps: 1. Prior to attaching BlueView to the front of the vehicle, ensure the bracket has rubber gaskets glued to them[cite: 8]. 2. Attach BlueView to the bracket, with the Impulse connector facing towards the back of the vehicle[cite: 8]. 3. Thread four stainless steel screws through the bracket[cite: 8]. 4. Apply Aqua Shield over all threads prior to adding washers and nuts[cite: 8]. 5. Add stainless steel washers, lock washers, and nuts, then tighten securely with 9/16” ratcheting wrenches[cite: 8].



Main Electronics Bottle - WHOI Engineered (1x)



Maintenance & Assembly Highlights: 1. Ensure vehicle power is completely off before removing[cite: 8]. 2. Disconnect all external bulkhead cables[cite: 8]. 3. Remove main bottle top clamps using a 9/16” ratcheting wrench and carefully transfer bottle onto its dedicated bench cradle[cite: 8]. 4. Remove the 4 outer threaded rods using a 7/16” wrench and pop the vacuum purge plug with a 3/16” hex key to release internal vacuum[cite: 8]. 5. Inspect internal fuses, replace desiccant packs (4 large packs), inspect and re-grease endcap O-rings with Molykote 55, and re-pull 16 inHg vacuum for 24 hours to verify stability[cite: 8].

title: Mechanical Weak Link Assembly
text:
The mechanical weak link protects the primary tow cable and ship winch from catastrophic over-tension during seafloor snags[cite: 8]. It is installed between the towing bridle and the mechanical cable clevis[cite: 6, 8].




[DROP WEAK LINK EXPLODED VIEW PHOTO HERE]  Weak Link Housing & Shear Pin Alignment


[DROP WEAK LINK ASSEMBLED PHOTO HERE]  Assembled Weak Link Attached to Tow Bridle






Assembly Procedure

Align the large holes on the outer housing with the large holes on the padeye inner housing (bridle), positioning set screws facing upwards[cite: 8]. Each side of the bridle and outer shell features one large hole and one small hole[cite: 8].
Slightly lift the bridle to slip the outer shell over the inner housing[cite: 8].
Rotate components until all matching holes align perfectly[cite: 8].
Insert the shear pin, wiggling the bridle and outer shell until the pin slides fully into position[cite: 8].
Ensure the shear pin is centered inside the body and sits completely flush on both sides[cite: 8].
Using a 3mm hex bit, tighten the set screws to 7.8 Nm to lock the pin flush[cite: 8]. (Note: Set torque on torque wrench prior to tightening)[cite: 8].
Attach the mechanical clevis to the weak link using the primary termination bolts[cite: 8]. Ensure the set screws remain secured and protected by a hose clamp[cite: 8].

title: Fiber Optic Termination (Clevis & Brooming)
text:
Purpose
Underwater fiber optic cables are used in environments where standard communication cables cannot provide the required durability, data capacity, or long-term reliability[cite: 8]. On the Henry B. Bigelow, the fiber optic cable run through the winch wire is cut annually, requiring a new fiber optic termination prior to survey deployment[cite: 8].



Termination Workflow

Part 1: Inserting the Fiber Optic into the Clevis

Mark and cut ~10m (33ft) off the ship’s fiber optic cable using a grinder and cutting wheel to discard stressed wire[cite: 8]. Place a hose clamp past the 33ft mark[cite: 8].
Measure and mark 24ft from the open end, placing another hose clamp[cite: 8].
Score outer shield wires with a Dremel, peel back armor wires to the score mark, and expose black inner jacketing[cite: 8].
Insert wire through the narrow end of the sandblasted clevis[cite: 8].



Part 2: Creating the Steel Broom



Steel Armor Wire Broom Formed and Seated inside Clevis Well



Fan armor wires out at 90° angles around the hose clamp to form a “broom”[cite: 8].
Walk clevis out to the aft deck, rig a come-along winch to deck padeyes, and draw 4–6 inches of the broom firmly into the clevis socket well[cite: 8].



Part 3: Epoxy Pouring

Wrap electrical/splicing tape around clevis top to build a 2–3 inch reservoir[cite: 8].
Mix Socketfast resin and catalyst thoroughly for 2 minutes[cite: 8].
Pour mixture into clevis well, tapping sides to release air bubbles[cite: 8]. Allow 24 hours room-temperature cure (or 30 mins at 180–200°F with heat guns)[cite: 8].





J-Box Integration & ST Connectorization

Part 4: The Boot & Fairing

Wrap 6 rolls of 2-inch self-vulcanizing tape to form a 2.5ft tapered boot from the clevis base[cite: 8].
Apply 18-inch heavy zip ties along the tow cable for 15–20 feet as fairing to eliminate cable vibration[cite: 8].



Part 5: J-Box Wiring & Oil Fill

Route power and fiber wires into J-box port, clamp internally with a hose clamp, and attach 12-10 AWG ring terminals to power wires[cite: 8].
Splice and polish singlemode fiber strands using 3M Hot Melt ST connectors (15-20 figure-8 passes on 9-micron gray sheet followed by green/white lapping films)[cite: 8]. Inspect under 200x scope for core chips or scratches[cite: 8].
Seal yellow urethane bladder, torque 5mm Allen screws evenly, and fill J-box completely with compensating oil using a vacuum pump[cite: 8].

title: Field Team Roles & Expectations
text:
1. Shift Structure & Overview
Cruise Manning Structure & Shift Operations: The HabCam scientific party typically consists of 9 to 10 personnel operating on 24-hour continuous sea trials divided into two 12-hour watch rotations (e.g., 11:30 AM to 11:30 PM and 11:30 PM to 11:30 AM)[cite: 7]. Each shift is managed by a Watch Chief and includes a rotating team of Pilots, Co-Pilots, and Annotators who cycle stations every 30 to 60 minutes to prevent screen fatigue[cite: 7]. The Chief Scientist maintains active oversight across both watches (6 AM to 6 PM baseline plus as-needed response)[cite: 7].

Manning / Shift
Primary High-Level Responsibilities

Population Dynamics

title: Field Team Roles & Expectations
text:
3. Detailed Role Specifications

Chief Scientist
As the Chief Scientist, you act as the primary liaison between the scientific party, the vessel’s crew, and shore-based support[cite: 7]. You must be prepared to make decisive, on-the-spot decisions at any time of day or night to ensure the success and safety of the mission[cite: 7].


HabCam Lead
As the HabCam Lead, you are the primary technical authority responsible for the deployment, operation, and data integrity of the imaging system[cite: 7]. You manage both the physical hardware of the vehicle and the IT infrastructure required to process its data[cite: 7].


Watch Chief
As a Watch Chief, you are the direct shift supervisor responsible for managing the personnel, operations, and data collection during your assigned rotation[cite: 7]. You ensure that scientific objectives are executed safely while maintaining data logging standards[cite: 7].


Pilot
You are directly responsible for the safe, precise, and active underwater navigation of the HabCam vehicle[cite: 7]. You operate in short, 30- to 60-minute focused intervals to maintain sharp reflexes[cite: 7].


Co-Pilot
Acts as the technical support partner and second pair of eyes for the Pilot to ensure flight safety, sonar obstacle analysis, and sensor telemetry health[cite: 7].
